d.title: A $46,000 bill is not actionable; 250 tokens per example is
d.caption: The whole method is to break the input down until each line is a decision. **"Few-shot examples are 2,500 tokens a call, which is $12,500 a month"** is something you can act on. The per-unit figures fall straight out and are what make the levers computable: 2,500 tokens over ten examples is **250 tokens per example**, so trimming to three is a calculable saving rather than a hope. And 10.6 already argued for logging the pieces: `prompt_tokens` alone tells you a spike happened and not which component caused it.

d.title: Four changes, 71% off, and none of them is a model change
d.caption: Each step is one of §01's lines reduced. **Reranking 8 chunks to 3 is the single largest lever at 41% cumulative**, because context was the largest component. Summarising history reaches 52%, and caching 40% of calls takes it to **71% — $46,000 down to $13,200** — without changing the model, the prompt's quality or the product. Which is the module's argument: the bill is mostly input tokens nobody audited.

d.title: Five ways to cut input tokens, and two of them improve quality
d.caption: The second row is the one worth noticing: **reranking to the top 3–5 instead of dumping 8 chunks also fixes lost-in-the-middle**, so it cuts cost *and* improves the answer — which is rare. Trimming few-shot examples usually costs nothing, because 2.2 measured two examples matching ten. And summarising history is the only lever that stops a cost from growing every turn rather than reducing a fixed one.

d.title: Four ways to cut output tokens, and the one that is billed differently
d.caption: Output is priced several times input, so these are worth more per token saved. **The stop-sequence row carries the detail people get wrong: you are billed for what is generated, not what you keep** — so trimming a response afterwards saves nothing and a stop sequence saves everything past it. And capping `max_tokens` does double duty, because 11.3 showed it bounds confabulation as well as cost.

d.title: A cascade is strictly more expensive than a router, always
d.caption: At 80% easy traffic and a 15× price gap, a **router** costs 25.3% of running everything on the strong model. A **cascade** costs that plus the cheap model's price on the escalated share — so it is **strictly more expensive, always, by exactly that amount**. The gap is 1.3 points here. What the premium buys is that **a cascade needs no classifier**: a router requires something that can predict difficulty *before* seeing an answer, and a cascade just tries the cheap model and checks.

nodes.label: The difference is the cheap call
But a cascade needs no classifier

d.title: One of these halves the bill and the other changes none of it
d.caption: The batch API is roughly **50% off for non-real-time work** — overnight summarisation, backfills, evaluation runs — and it is the largest single discount available for changing nothing but the deadline. **Streaming reduces no tokens and no cost whatsoever.** It slashes *perceived* latency, which 9.15 measured as the difference between reading along at 400 ms and staring at a spinner for 5.4 seconds — a real product win and not a line on the invoice.
cells: for work nobody is waiting on

d.title: Meter in the smallest unit the price can express
d.caption: At $5 per million input tokens a **single token costs $0.000005**, so six decimal places is the smallest unit that can represent one token at all. That matters because the metered value accumulates: a per-call rounding error of $0.000005 over a million calls a month is $5 — noise — but the same reasoning applied to a cent-rounded meter loses far more. **Meter in the smallest unit the price can express, and round only at display time.**

nodes.label: Round per call and it accumulates

d.title: The scenario a per-user cap cannot see
d.caption: Four scenarios, and **a per-user cap fires on exactly one of them.** The buggy client looping is caught, correctly, at $1,100 for one user. Traffic growing tenfold is not caught and should not be — per-user spend is unchanged. And the last row is the one that matters: **prompt bloat takes the bill from $396 to $972 with nothing about the request pattern changed** — same users, same call counts, same latency, same per-user figure at $0.97. No per-user cap can see it, which is why 10.3 lists **cost per request** as an alert.

d.title: Six scopes, and what only each one catches
d.caption: The scopes are not redundant — each catches something the others cannot. **A per-run cap is the only thing that stops an agent loop**, because 11.10's per-call limit cannot see twenty calls that are each within budget. **A per-feature cost-per-request alert is the only thing that sees prompt bloat**, which §02 measured as invisible to every other control. And the global kill switch catches everything you did not predict, which is its whole purpose.

d.title: Eight risks, and the guardrail that is primary for each
d.caption: Read the right-hand column: **two of these need something other than a scan.** Hallucination needs a grounding guard, which is 11.4 to 11.6 and not a filter at all. And an unsafe action by an agent needs **least-privilege tools plus human approval** — a structural control, because no amount of input scanning stops a model from asking to do something it is permitted to do. The first row's parenthesis is the one most designs miss: injection arrives in a retrieved document as well as in user text.

d.title: Your input scan sees a harmless question
d.caption: **Direct injection arrives in the user's message, where you expect it and scan for it. Indirect injection arrives in a document your system retrieved** — and this is the risk RAG introduces that a naive guardrail design misses completely. The input scan sees *"what is the refund policy?"* and passes it, correctly; the instruction is in chunk 3. The structural defence is the fourth input guardrail: **wrap untrusted content in explicit delimiters and tell the model everything inside them is data.**

nodes.label: The scan sees a harmless question

d.title: A pattern list is a tripwire for the laziest attempts
d.caption: The paraphrases that got through include *"Forget everything you were told before this message"* and *"The instructions above no longer apply"*. **None of those requires a sophisticated attacker** — they are the ordinary ways a person phrases the same intent, which is the structural problem with a pattern list: the intent has unbounded surface forms and the list has a finite number of entries. So *first layer, not a solution* understates it. It is worth having because **it costs 0.2 ms**, not because it works.

nodes.label: Keep it for the cost, not the coverage

d.title: PII regexes fail in both directions, measured
d.caption: **Names and addresses pass straight through** — *"My name is Venu Kiran and I live at 14 Mill Lane, Bristol"* is unredacted, because no regex describes a name. And in the other direction, **an internal ticket number of SSN shape is redacted anyway**: *"Reference 123-45-6789 is our internal ticket number"* becomes *"Reference [SSN]"*, destroying the thing the user was asking about. One expectation also failed: the phone pattern does **not** shadow the SSN pattern, because it needs three digits after the separator.

steps.code: a name and a street address

d.title: Toxicity is harder than injection for a pattern list, not easier
d.caption: The recommendation is a dedicated moderation model rather than hand-rolled regex, and 11.13's measurement is why — with the direction people get backwards. **Toxicity has even more open-ended surface forms than injection and far more benign collisions**, so a regex both misses more and over-blocks more. The **per-category structure** matters too: a single *unsafe* score cannot support different thresholds for self-harm and illegal-activity content, and those thresholds are genuinely different policy decisions.

d.title: The canary is the only check here with no threshold
d.caption: Plant a unique secret string in the system prompt; **if it appears in the output, the model reproduced part of its system prompt — there is no other way for that string to exist.** Compare the others: moderation has a threshold and a precision/recall trade-off, and PII regexes have the false positives 11.13 measured. The canary's limitation is the mirror image of theirs: **near-zero false positives and a high false-negative rate**, because a model that paraphrases its instructions rather than quoting them leaves no trace.

d.title: The context parameter goes into the model untouched
d.caption: Reading the pipeline carefully: `scan_input` runs on `user_input` and `redact` runs on `user_input` — and **the `context` parameter goes straight into the model untouched.** So the pipeline that exists to defend against injection has **no defence against the indirect injection of 11.12**, which is the form RAG introduces. That is less an inconsistency than a demonstration of how easy the gap is to leave: the function reads as complete, and every check is present. The fix is two lines, and it has to be noticed first.

nodes.label: The function reads as complete
nodes.sub: which is why it is missed

nodes.label: Two lines: scan it, and wrap both as data

d.title: The free checks are 2.4 ms of a 3,134 ms request
d.caption: The jailbreak scan, PII redaction, canary check, secrets scan and schema validation together cost **2.4 ms on a 3,134 ms request — 0.08%**. So any argument against running all of them is not a latency argument. The budget discussion is entirely about the **model-based** checks, and there the arithmetic is real: sequential input and output gates total 138.4 ms, and **parallelising within each stage takes that to 73.0 ms — a 47% cut on guardrail latency and 2.1% of the request.**

d.title: Over-refusal is invisible by default, and that asymmetry drives the tuning
d.caption: Six of ten benign-but-tricky inputs blocked, **precision 0.571 — so nearly half of everything the regex scan blocked was a real user.** What makes this insidious is the visibility asymmetry: **a harmful answer that escapes generates a complaint, a screenshot and an incident; a wrongly refused question generates a shrug and a lost user.** Teams tighten in response to the failures they see and never loosen in response to the ones they do not, so the threshold ratchets in one direction only.

nodes.label: Only one of them is visible
So the threshold ratchets one way
Which is why you measure both

d.title: A threshold moved by 0.1 changes both error rates by a factor of two
d.caption: **F1 picks 0.50 and F1 is the wrong objective**, because it weights the two errors equally and for a safety guardrail they are almost never equal. The curve is also steep: moving 0.5 to 0.8 cuts over-refusal from 6.0% to **0.1%** and lets harmful-miss rise from 10.3% to **67.7%**. So the sweep is a **policy choice, not an optimisation**, and the honest framing states both numbers: *at 0.5 we miss 10.3% of harmful content and wrongly refuse 6.0% of legitimate requests.*

d.title: Six metrics, and the two where any value above zero is an incident
d.caption: **Block rate cannot tell you what a spike means** — an attack and a broken guardrail look identical — which is why §02 pairs it with precision. Two rows have no threshold at all: **a PII leak event and a canary hit are each an incident**, because there is no acceptable rate. And the last row is 11.15's measurement: the free checks cost 0.1% of a request, so moderation latency is a conversation about model-based checks only.

cells.text: an attack, or a broken guardrail

cells: high means guardrails are hurting the product

d.title: Every useful metric here is a pair
d.caption: A single number in this module is always ambiguous, and the pairing resolves it. **Jailbreak success against over-refusal** move in opposite directions at roughly a ten-to-one exchange rate — 11.16's curve. **Block rate against precision** separates an attack from a broken guardrail, which block rate alone confounds. And **abstention rate against context recall** is 11.6's finding: a 0.30 abstention rate means something completely different with weak recall than with good recall.

d.title: Assume yes, fail closed, and tune both directions
d.caption: **"Assume YES for any user-facing LLM"** — there is no version of a user-facing application where untrusted text does not reach the model, so the first question is not really a question. The *retrieved content* clause in the fourth input step is the one 11.15 found missing from the implementation. Output guardrails **fail closed**: any failure routes to a safe response rather than passing through. And the last line is the module's thesis compressed: **tune for harmful false negatives AND over-refusal false positives.**
